The following text is adapted from Jacob Riis’s 1901 autobiography The Making of an American. Riis, a twenty-one-year-old carpenter from Denmark, describes arriving in New York City by ship in 1870.

It was a beautiful spring morning, and as I looked over the rail at the miles of straight streets, the green heights of Brooklyn, and the stir of ferryboats and pleasure craft on the river, my hopes rose high that somewhere in this teeming hive there would be a place for me. What kind of a place I had myself no clear notion of. I would let that work out as it could. The love of change belongs to youth, and I meant to take a hand in things as they came along.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why the narrator decided to give up his work as a carpenter
To describe the hardships the narrator faced during his long voyage
To compare New York with the town where the narrator grew up
To convey the narrator’s hopeful outlook as he arrives in a new country
items.explanation: Looking at New York from the ship, the narrator says “my hopes rose high that somewhere in this teeming hive there would be a place for me.” Although he has “no clear notion” of what that place will be, he means “to take a hand in things as they came along.” The text conveys his hopeful outlook on arriving, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The context line says Riis was a carpenter, but the excerpt never explains any decision to give up that work.

B.why_wrong: The excerpt begins as the ship arrives on “a beautiful spring morning”; it does not describe the voyage or any hardships.

C.why_wrong: The narrator describes only what he sees of New York and Brooklyn; he never mentions or compares the town where he grew up.

sources.what: Riis, The Making of an American (1901), chapter 2 (“I Land in New York”), opening paragraph, adapted by cutting sentences

items.notes: Literature (autobiography, 1901). Key D. Adapted: the excerpt starts at “It was a beautiful spring morning” and drops one sentence (“Of course I had my trade to fall back on, …”) before “The love of change.” Riis was born in 1849 and arrived on the Iowa at Whitsunday 1870. Writer's own blind solve: D.

items.passage: Fela Sowande was a Nigerian composer and organist. Born in 1905 in Abeokuta, he moved to London in 1934 to study music and later became a fellow of the Royal College of Organists. Sowande’s compositions combine African and European musical traditions. His organ pieces, for example, borrow the style of English church music while incorporating the five-note melodies of traditional Yoruba songs. His African Suite, composed for string orchestra, similarly combines European forms with African rhythms and harmonies.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a disagreement between two musicians and then explains how it was settled.
It explains a musical technique and then lists several composers who use it.
It introduces a composer and then describes some qualities of his music.
It compares two composers and then argues that one of them was more influential.
items.explanation: The text first introduces Fela Sowande, giving his birthplace and training. It then describes his compositions, which “combine African and European musical traditions,” with examples from his organ pieces and his African Suite. Choice C describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: The text discusses only Sowande and describes no disagreement.

B.why_wrong: The text is about one composer, not a technique used by several composers.

D.why_wrong: No second composer is mentioned, and the text makes no argument about influence.

sources.what: Fela Sowande: born 1905 in Abeokuta; went to London in 1934; Fellow of the Royal College of Organists (1943); Western and African ideas in his music; organ works combine Anglican church music with Yoruba pentatonic melodies; African Suite for string orchestra; orchestral works show African rhythmic and harmonic characteristics (Wikipedia)

items.notes: Area: humanities (music). Key C. Easy structure as in 1.13 and 1.19 (a person, then characteristics of the work).

items.passage: Historians studying slavery frequently have few sources written from the perspective of enslaved people themselves. Court records can help fill that gap. <u>In her 2019 book Voices of the Enslaved, for example, historian Sophie White examines testimony that enslaved men and women delivered before the Superior Council, the highest court of French colonial Louisiana, during the 1700s.</u> Because court clerks documented these statements in considerable detail, they preserve individuals’ own descriptions of their work, their relationships, and their aspirations.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence?
options: It gives an example of a historian using the type of source named in the previous sentence.
It explains why many of the court records from French colonial Louisiana were later lost.
It argues that court records are more reliable sources than the letters or diaries of the period.
It describes a problem that the rest of the text then tries to solve.
items.explanation: The previous sentence says that “Court records can help fill that gap.” The underlined sentence gives an example: Sophie White’s book “examines testimony that enslaved men and women delivered before the Superior Council.” The underlined sentence therefore provides an example of a historian using court records, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The text says the clerks’ records “preserve individuals’ own descriptions” of their lives; it says nothing about records being lost.

C.why_wrong: The text never compares court records with letters or diaries.

D.why_wrong: The problem, a shortage of sources, appears in the first sentence; the underlined sentence gives an example of a way around it.

sources.what: Frederick Douglass Book Prize committee on Sophie White's Voices of the Enslaved: trial records from the Louisiana Superior Council, French New Orleans; enslaved people telling their own stories in court

items.notes: Area: history. Key A. Easy example item as in 1.3 (sources, then one such source). Published 2019 by the Omohundro Institute and UNC Press; testimony from 1723 to 1769 survives.

items.passage: Many tarantulas display a vivid blue coloration, which is puzzling because these spiders perceive color poorly and do not perform visual displays when courting. To investigate, Bor-Kai Hsiung and colleagues examined the hairs of blue tarantulas representing many branches of the group’s evolutionary tree. They discovered that the blue is produced by microscopic structures in the hairs rather than by pigment, and that these structures differ considerably among species. Yet the shade of blue is remarkably consistent, suggesting that the coloration evolved independently many times and probably serves some function other than attracting mates.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It describes an experiment testing whether tarantulas can see the color blue.
It presents a study that addresses a puzzling feature of some spiders.
It explains how tarantulas use their blue color to attract mates.
It compares the colors of tarantulas with the colors of other spiders.
items.explanation: The text begins with a puzzle: many tarantulas are blue even though they “perceive color poorly.” It then describes how Hsiung and colleagues studied the hairs of blue tarantulas and what they found about where the color comes from and how it evolved. Choice B states this purpose.

A.why_wrong: The text states that tarantulas perceive color poorly, but the study it describes examined the spiders’ hairs, not their vision.

C.why_wrong: The researchers concluded that the coloration probably serves “some function other than attracting mates.”

D.why_wrong: The text compares blue tarantula species with one another, not tarantulas with other spiders.

sources.what: Hsiung et al. (2015, Science Advances): blue in phylogenetically distant tarantulas peaks in a narrow band near 450 nm; produced by different nanostructures (quasi-ordered and multilayer); poor color perception and no conspicuous courtship display argue the color is not sexually selected; convergence

items.notes: Area: natural science (biology). Key B. Easy study item as in 1.15 (an open question, a study, its finding). “Evolved many separate times” is the paper's convergence finding stated plainly.

items.passage: When a tree dies in a managed forest, it is frequently removed to keep the woodland tidy. That practice deserves reconsideration. Dead wood is far from useless: by some estimates, up to 40 percent of forest animals depend on it. Woodpeckers and other birds nest in hollow trunks, mosses and fungi colonize fallen logs, and decomposing wood returns nutrients to the soil while retaining moisture during droughts. Leaving dead trees where they fall is one of the simplest ways to maintain a healthy forest.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe how woodpeckers build their nests inside dead trees
To explain how forest managers decide which trees to cut down
To argue that dead trees should be left in forests
To compare the health of managed forests with that of wild forests
items.explanation: The text says that the practice of removing dead trees “deserves reconsideration” and lists the ways dead wood supports forest life. It ends by saying that “Leaving dead trees where they fall is one of the simplest ways to maintain a healthy forest.” The text therefore argues that dead trees should be left in forests, as choice C says.

A.why_wrong: The text mentions that birds nest in hollow trunks only as one example of how dead wood is used; it does not describe how woodpeckers build nests.

B.why_wrong: The text says dead trees are frequently removed but never explains how managers choose which trees to cut.

D.why_wrong: The text does not compare managed forests with wild ones.

sources.what: Coarse woody debris: up to forty percent of forest fauna dependent on it; a third of woodland birds nest in cavities of dead trunks; mosses, lichens and ferns on logs; nutrient recycling; slows evaporation of soil moisture; managed woods hold less fallen debris; leaving dead wood considered best practice (Wikipedia)

items.notes: Area: natural science (forest ecology). Key C. Explicit argument with evaluative language (“deserves to change”), as in 1.22. The 40 percent figure is hedged (“by some estimates”) as the source gives it (“up to”).

items.passage: Are whale sharks, the largest fish in the ocean, exclusively carnivorous? <u>A 2022 study led by marine biologist Mark Meekan suggests they are not.</u> Whale sharks feed by filtering enormous volumes of water, and scientists had assumed that any seaweed they swallowed along with the tiny animals they consume simply passed through their bodies undigested. But chemical analyses of tissue from whale sharks off Western Australia revealed that the sharks were digesting a floating seaweed called Sargassum. The researchers concluded that whale sharks are omnivores, making them the largest known omnivores on Earth.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It introduces a claim that the researchers’ findings later contradict.
It provides an answer to the question in the previous sentence.
It describes the method the researchers used to study the sharks’ diet.
It explains why whale sharks need to eat such large amounts of food.
items.explanation: The first sentence asks whether whale sharks are “exclusively carnivorous.” The underlined sentence answers it: a 2022 study “suggests they are not.” The rest of the text explains the evidence for that answer. Choice B describes this function.

A.why_wrong: The findings described later support the underlined sentence; they show that the sharks digest seaweed.

C.recipe: wrong part: the method comes later (PART)
C.why_wrong: The method, chemical analysis of tissue, is described two sentences later, not in the underlined sentence.

D.why_wrong: The text never explains why whale sharks need large amounts of food.

sources.what: Meekan et al. (2022, Ecology), “The world's largest omnivore is a fish”: whale shark trophic level consistent with omnivory (amino acid isotopes); fatty acids show floating Sargassum and its epibionts as a significant food source

items.notes: Area: natural science (marine biology). Key B. Easy F_answer as in 1.18 (a question, then the underlined answer). The study used whale sharks at Ningaloo Reef, Western Australia.
